summary: Interlude (2003 Northeast Blackout) answered. The XA/21 alarm system's race condition produced a SILENT failure: the alarm thread froze, the queue filled, new alarms were discarded, but the display subsystem kept showing a frozen-but-green picture. Operators had 'no reason to doubt their instruments' -- the instruments were not lying, they simply stopped speaking. The lesson lands directly on the fork work: (1) A system that reports stale data as if it were live is worse than a system that reports nothing, because a loud failure triggers investigation while a silent one looks normal. In the cache race I fixed, the stale-populate-after-invalidate bug was exactly this class: the redirect cache served an old URL as if it were current, and only the version token (INCR on invalidate + reject mismatch on read) converted a silent staleness into a verifiable truth. (2) Monitoring must monitor the monitor: the alarm subsystem itself had no heartbeat/watchdog, so its own failure was invisible; the equivalent lesson is that a cache read path must be able to distinguish a populated entry from a stale one. (3) The cost compounds over time -- 90+ minutes of warning existed but was invisible, and 'everything is fine' from operators who believed their screens cost 55 million people power. (4) The fix hierarchy: redundant/divergent signal sources beat a single source of truth; in the fork, the DB is the source of truth and the cache is only a performance layer, so correctness must always fall back to the DB when version disagreement is detected. The module's transition from Incident Response (M5) to Multi-Layer Bugs (M6) is earned: this story is a multi-layer bug where the alarm layer, the display layer, and the real-world electrical layer all disagreed, and the operators had no cross-layer check to catch it.
evidence: Interlude lesson: silent failure vs loud failure; stale data shown as live
Link to fork work: version-token cache fix converts silent staleness to verifiable truth
Monitoring-the-monitor lesson: heartbeat/watchdog for alarm systems and cache coherence
